records.text: How my docotoral journey began Six months ago, my doctoral thesis was finally published. I needed some distance first. Time to realise that this chapter was really finished and to put it away for a while. Now I’m ready to share its contents and findings. I also want to share some of the journey behind it, because pursuing a doctorate alongside my professional role was not always easy. Working between Munich and Tokyo for many years has given me first hand experience of how communication and relationship building differ across cultures. This experience shaped my research. Germany and Japan are both highly advanced manufacturing economies. What I wanted to understand was how decision makers build and sustain trust across a growing variety of communication channels. 💡 Which communication channels do decision makers and next generation professionals in German and Japanese SMEs actually use when buying machine tools or automation solutions, and why? 💡 What makes them trust one channel over another, and how do cultural and generational differences influence this? 💡 How do we maintain human connection as industrial communication becomes increasingly digital? For my research, I spoke with decision makers in Germany and Japan and also with the next generation who will make these decisions in the future. The findings confirmed something I had experienced throughout my professional life: industrial communication remains fundamentally shaped by human interaction, even as digitisation advances. I want to share this knowledge because these questions are relevant for our industry and I believe many companies are asking similar questions today. So this is the start of a series. Over the coming weeks, I will share some of the findings of my research and some reflections of my journey.

records.title: MathWorks
records.text: In my last post here, I created a simulation of a robot arm (from Onshape by PTC ) that uses 4DOF and a pencil-like end effector to transcribe spoken or recorded audio into real Braille inside MathWorks Simscape. Braille characters are tactile reading symbols built from a standard six-dot cell arranged in two vertical columns of three dots. Naturally, I let my imagination run wild and created a tactile Braille reader too. It uses the same robot arm with an extra DOF that allows it to slide while reading, much like how real Braille would be read. It has three prongs on a finger that register a pulse anytime any prong touches a Braille dot. These pulses are converted into six-dot cells to form Unicode characters. Each character is sent with all previously read characters to the liblouis translator, which translates the Braille bytes back into readable English text. The most interesting lesson I learned while implementing this project is that the meaning of a Braille character can change depending on which characters are read before or after it! Cheers to learning new things every day. I just might end up trying this in hardware someday. Enjoy the demo below!

records.title: UNIGINE
records.text: Navigation & Pathfinding has been completely reworked in UNIGINE Engine 2.22. The new experimental system is designed for large, dynamic worlds, with double-precision world coordinates to keep navigation accurate even across very large environments. Together, these improvements provide a much more scalable and flexible foundation for NPCs and other autonomous characters navigating complex simulation and game environments. You can now: • Generate NavMeshes automatically from scene geometry • Stream navigation data across large open worlds • Rebuild only affected areas when the environment changes • Generate navigation data at runtime for procedural or dynamic environments • Define cost-weighted areas, so characters can prefer roads, avoid rough terrain or hazards, and stay out of restricted zones • Handle dynamic obstacles without rebuilding the whole NavMesh • Use multithreaded pathfinding for large numbers of characters • Keep characters on route toward moving targets with path corridors • Run crowd avoidance with priorities and interaction rules • Profile navigation memory usage and per-frame performance directly in the engine For large-scale environments, you can also combine different levels of navigation detail — for example, keeping a coarse NavMesh for the whole world while streaming or generating higher-detail navigation around active characters. The new system is available as an experimental feature in UNIGINE SDK 2.22.

records.title: Vertical Aerospace
records.text: What was the aircraft mass/MTOW, flight condition and power setting? Was this hover, take-off, approach or flyover? What was the measurement distance, microphone position and atmospheric condition? Was the test conducted in an acoustically open area, and how far away were the nearest reflecting surfaces? A single dB number is not an adequate description of aircraft noise. I would like to see the 1/3-octave-band SPL spectrum, together with the broadband and discrete tonal components. Propeller/rotor blade-passage frequencies and their harmonics can have a disproportionately high effect on perceived annoyance even when the overall SPL appears relatively modest. And the urban environment matters enormously. Buildings, façades and the ground introduce reflections, reverberation and, at particular frequencies and locations, constructive interference, producing local sound levels quite different from those measured in an open-field test. So comparing “<50 dB Valo” with “55 dB dishwasher” is visually attractive, but acoustically it is potentially very misleading. Noise is not just “how many dB?” It is how much, at what frequencies, for how long, under what operating condition, and measured where.

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or gov
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, n
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA

records.text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. This is one of the missions behind ZEE, and behind everything my extraordinary team builds: a world where every single flight reaches its destination safely. Full post: https://lnkd.in/dvauVg2E.

records.text: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Read On particle dynamics in steady axial rotor flows, published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics: https://lnkd.in/eys6i2qJ #AerospaceEngineering #Polimi.

records.text: Организация Sarla Aviation разместила контент: They say an airworthiness engineer is a jack of all trades and master of none. Devarasu Kannan sees it differently: to do the job properly, you have to be a master of many. Kannan has spent 32 years in Indian aviation. He started with seven years at the DGCA, then spent 25 years at the National Aerospace Laboratories working on HANSA-3, HANSA-NG, C-NM5 and SARAS. Over that time he dealt with every authority an aircraft has to answer to, from the DGCA to CEMILAC and DGAQA, and getting approvals on time was the work he was proudest of. He first came to Sarla as an advisor to help write our Design Organisation Manual. In his words, other teams had the talent but worked "like a student project." At Sarla he saw the work being run in project mode. We received our Design Organisation Approval on 7th August 2026, within six months, which Kannan says he never managed to do before. He now leads airworthiness at Sarla and is still learning. "Learning is a journey, not a destination. Every day technology changes, requirements change, regulations change. That is the mantra." Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA
